 'Same Old Way' features 12 unreleased songs recorded between 1986 and 2013, restored by producer Kyle Lehning
 By
 Christina Dugan Ramirez Fox News

 close Video Randy Travis’ wife says doctors gave country legend 1% chance of survival before miraculous comeback 
 Randy Travis' wife Mary reveals the emotional journey from a 1% survival chance to releasing "Same Old Way" more than a decade after his stroke.
 NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!
 Randy Travis' life was turned upside down by a devastating health crisis that doctors gave him just a 1% chance of surviving, according to his wife, Mary.
 In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, the country legend — whose new 12-track album, "Same Old Way," is out now — and his wife, Mary, reflected on that life-changing ordeal more than a decade ago, explained how hope and faith played a pivotal role in his recovery, and shared how his determination helped him rebuild his life and reconnect with music.
 "They had already told us he had 1% chance of survival. And that was the first couple of days in the hospital," Mary said. "So here we are, five and a half months later, he's still here. He's still improving. We went through the second brain surgery. He came through that with flying colors. The first one is when they said he's not, you know, he doesn't have any chance. But, you know, once you get over those and you start seeing the glimmers of hope and the hand of God on the whole thing."
 RANDY TRAVIS' HEALTH CRISIS BEGAN WITH 'CONGESTION' AND ENDED IN A FIVE-MONTH HOSPITAL STAY 
 Randy Travis' wife, Mary, says the country legend was given a 1% chance of survival in 2013. (Getty Images for the Grand Ole Opry) 
 The "Forever and Ever, Amen" singer was hospitalized in 2013 for congestive heart failure tied to viral cardiomyopathy. He subsequently suffered a massive stroke that left him with partial paralysis and affected his speech. What began as a trip to seek treatment for congestion became a five-and-a-half-month hospital stay, followed by years of rehabilitation.
 "We went through three years of rehab every single day, so we were very quiet and out of the limelight, if you will," she added. "We, you know, we were at home. We went to rehab every day for about three years."
 Travis won many awards throughout his 40 years in the music industry, including seven Grammy Awards. (Oscar Abolafia/TPLP/Getty Images) 
 Eventually, Mary said, Travis "got tired" of the constant rehabilitation and decided to "go live life." Their trips back to Nashville helped renew their hope that he could once again be involved in the music he loved.
 WATCH: RANDY TRAVIS’ WIFE SAYS DOCTORS GAVE COUNTRY LEGEND 1% CHANCE OF SURVIVAL BEFORE MIRACULOUS COMEBACK 
 Video Travis has since found new ways to share his music and connect with fans. In May 2024, he released "Where That Came From," using AI technology to recreate his signature singing voice. His "More Life" tour continued through 2026, with Travis appearing alongside Mary while guest vocalist James Dupré and his longtime band perform his hits.
 VINCE GILL GAVE AMY GRANT A REALITY CHECK DURING RECOVERY FROM BRAIN INJURY 
 Mary previously told Fox News Digital that Randy's health crisis cemented their relationship. (Amy E. Price/Getty Images) 
 Now, with the release of his first album of original material in more than 18 years — featuring 12 previously unreleased songs recorded between 1986 and 2013 and restored by his longtime producer, Kyle Lehning — Mary is reflecting on the determination and gratitude that carried her husband through his toughest moments.
 CELINE DION BREAKS DOWN ONSTAGE DURING EMOTIONAL RETURN AFTER 6-YEAR HIATUS 
 "Just being with this guy has been such an inspiration to me because, going through even the tough times in the hospital, the nurses would come in and cut him or stick him or poke him or do whatever, and they'd walk out the door. And if he wasn't in his coma and he was aware, he’d say, ‘Thank you.’ That was Randy Travis," she said. "And they'd turn around and look like, you got to be kidding me, you know. But that was Randy Travis ."
 Randy Travis, Mary Travis and James Dupré visit the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville, Tenn., on March 5, 2025. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images) 
 That same spirit, she said, followed him into rehabilitation and remains evident today, even as aphasia continues to affect his ability to communicate.
 "I have pictures of him there in the rehab center and he's smiling. He's laughing. He’s giving it all he's got. Randy Travis hasn't changed. And that's still the man that I get to sit beside right now," she said. "He still has that, that love for life, the love for people."
 For Mary, the release of "Same Old Way" is especially emotional because it represents an opportunity they once weren't sure would ever come again. Before his stroke, she said, they assumed there would be many more albums and years of making music ahead.
 BILLY RAY CYRUS CHEATED DEATH DURING SEPSIS, VOCAL PARALYSIS BATTLE BEFORE STAGING MUSIC COMEBACK 
 Travis' new album, "Same Old Way," was released Nov. 13. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images) 
 "It's really an emotional thing, because 18 years ago when he put out his last one, we thought that the world was an oyster and there was gonna be so many more," she said. "But the stroke happened, it was 13 years ago, and everything changed."
 "Thirteen years ago, we had no idea, based on where we were then, when we were in the hospital, that we would have this opportunity. So, in a way, it’s a miracle," she added. "I get emotional when I think about it, just because I wanted to hear his voice so bad again."
 Randy Travis and James Dupre perform during the Volunteer Jam: A Musical Salute to Charlie Daniels at Bridgestone Arena in Nashville, Tenn., on Aug. 18, 2021. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images) 
 Hearing those recordings, Mary explained, offers listeners a chance to experience Travis' voice at different stages of his life — and gives the couple another reason to appreciate how far he has come.

 "Life is so precious and so fragile, but it’s so wonderful also. And to be able to do something like this, it’s pretty monumental," she said. "It doesn't happen often that somebody has the opportunity to do this after a life-changing moment."
 Christina Dugan Ramirez is an entertainment journalist with more than 15 years of experience, including a decade at PEOPLE writing high-profile cover stories, covering Hollywood's biggest events, and interviewing many of the industry's most influential stars before joining Fox News Digital in 2024.
